subChunks.title: IoC Container & Dependency Injection

storyBeats.text: You have entered the realm of Spring — the most powerful framework in the Java kingdom.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Before Spring, wizards conjured every dependency themselves — a nightmare of tangled creation code. The IoC container conjures them for you, in the right order, every time.

storyBeats.label: Field injection vs constructor injection

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create a GreetingService that depends on a MessageProvider interface. Implement MessageProvider with a class that returns "Hello, Wizard!". Use constructor injection. Print the greeting.
guidedPractice.hint: GreetingService takes MessageProvider via constructor. greet() calls provider.getMessage() and prints it.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the IoC principle. Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?

questions.prompt: Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection in Spring?
options: Dependencies are explicit, the object is always fully initialised, and it is easy to test
Constructor injection is faster at runtime
questions.answer: Dependencies are explicit, the object is always fully initialised, and it is easy to test
questions.explanation: Constructor injection makes dependencies visible and allows the class to be used outside Spring (e.g., in unit tests).

questions.prompt: @Autowired on a field is generally recommended for production Spring code.
questions.explanation: Field injection hides dependencies and makes testing harder. Constructor injection is preferred.

questions.prompt: You want to swap the database implementation in tests without changing your service. What pattern enables this?
options: Depend on the interface, use constructor injection. In tests, pass a mock or in-memory implementation. Spring injects the real JPA impl in production.
Use @Autowired on the field and change the implementation class
Create a subclass of the service for testing
questions.answer: Depend on the interface, use constructor injection. In tests, pass a mock or in-memory implementation. Spring injects the real JPA impl in production.
questions.explanation: This is the power of DI + programming to interfaces — easy substitution without changing the service.

subChunks.title: Spring Beans & Configuration

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Use @Service/@Repository/@Component for your own classes. Use @Bean in @Configuration for objects you can't annotate — like ObjectMapper or HikariDataSource.
Component scan is Spring Boot's magic — it automatically detects all @Component-annotated classes in your package and registers them as beans.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Write a @Configuration class with a @Bean method that returns a StringBuilder initialised with "Arcane: ". Then show (in a main method) how you would use it.
guidedPractice.hint: AppConfig.arcaneBuilder() returns new StringBuilder("Arcane: "). Then append "Academy" and print.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: When would you use @Bean in a @Configuration class instead of @Component? Give two examples.

questions.prompt: What is the default bean scope in Spring?
questions.explanation: Spring beans are singleton by default. Use @Scope("prototype") for a new instance on each injection.

questions.prompt: You need to configure a third-party HttpClient with custom timeout settings. Which approach is correct?
options: @Bean method in @Configuration returning the configured HttpClient
Create it in each service that needs it
questions.answer: @Bean method in @Configuration returning the configured HttpClient
questions.explanation: You can't add @Component to a class you don't own. Use @Bean in @Configuration to configure and expose third-party instances.

subChunks.title: Aspect-Oriented Programming

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: AOP is like enchanting a doorway — every spell that passes through it gets logged, timed, or checked, without any spell knowing the enchantment exists. @Transactional works this way.
Spring's @Transactional annotation is AOP in action — Spring wraps your method in a transaction proxy without you writing a single try/commit/rollback.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Simulate AOP manually: create a ServiceProxy that wraps a Calculator and logs before and after calling add(int a, int b). Print the log and result.
guidedPractice.hint: LoggingCalculator.add() prints "Before: add", delegates to real calculator, prints "After: add", returns result.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain AOP. Name three real-world uses of AOP in Spring applications.

questions.prompt: Which Spring annotation is implemented using AOP under the hood?
questions.explanation: Spring's @Transactional wraps methods in a transaction via an AOP proxy — begin, proceed, commit/rollback.

questions.prompt: @Around advice can prevent the target method from executing at all.
questions.explanation: @Around receives a ProceedingJoinPoint — calling proceed() runs the method. You can choose not to call it.

subChunks.title: Spring Events & Environment Abstraction

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Events are the whisper network of the Academy. OrderService announces an order was placed — it doesn't care who listens. Email, Inventory, Analytics — each handler subscribes independently.

storyBeats.label: @Value usage
storyBeats.code:
@Value("${app.max-retries:3}")
private int maxRetries; // reads from application.yml, defaults to 3

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Simulate Spring events without the framework: create an EventBus with publish(String event) and subscribe(Consumer<String> handler). Publish "OrderPlaced" and print it from two subscribers.
guidedPractice.hint: handlers is a List<Consumer<String>>. subscribe() adds to the list. publish() calls each handler.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Spring Application Events. What decoupling benefit do they provide over direct method calls?

questions.prompt: What annotation marks a method as a Spring event listener?
questions.explanation: @EventListener on a method in a Spring bean registers it to receive matching application events.

questions.prompt: @Value can inject values from application.yml into Spring beans.
questions.explanation: @Value("${property.name}") reads properties from the Spring Environment (application.yml, env vars, etc.).
